issue: Can reasonable suspicion for an investigatory stop rest on an anonymous tip that police corroborate only as to innocent details, or must the corroborated facts point to criminal activity?

sides.position: Reasonable suspicion requires corroboration of the tip that points to criminal activity; corroborated innocent conduct alone does not suffice (the criminal-corroboration rule, as described in the dissent).
cases: United States v. Norbert, No. 20-60106 (5th Cir. 2021)

sides.position: Reasonable suspicion of criminal activity may be formed by observing exclusively legal activity, and it need not rule out the possibility of innocent conduct.
cases: United States v. Wanjiku, 919 F.3d 472 (7th Cir. 2019)
United States v. Matchett, 802 F.3d 1185 (11th Cir. 2015)
United States v. Diaz, 802 F.3d 234 (2d Cir. 2015)
United States v. Alvarez, 899 F.2d 833 (9th Cir. 1990)

this_court: Adopts the criminal-corroboration rule, under which corroborated innocent details do not establish reasonable suspicion (as the dissent characterizes the majority's holding).
quote: Second, the majority’s criminal-corroboration rule creates a circuit split.
cite: United States v. Norbert, No. 20-60106 (5th Cir. 2021)
